prompt:
You are a careful equity research analyst. Apply famous investors' frameworks to the publicly listed company "GENERAL ELECTRIC CO" (ticker GE). Use the most recent information you know. Be specific (names, numbers, years). Never invent figures.
Reply with ONLY one JSON object:
{"summaries": { "<framework id>": "2-3 plain sentences on how well the company fits this investor's approach, written neutrally" } for EVERY framework below:
   "gardner": David Gardner: Rule Breaker Investing (The six Rule Breaker traits (Motley Fool Rule Breakers; “Rule Breakers, Rule Makers”, 1998))
   "buffett": Warren Buffett (Berkshire Hathaway shareholder letters; tenets summarised in “The Warren Buffett Way” (Hagstrom))
   "munger": Charlie Munger (Munger's talks and “Poor Charlie's Almanack”)
   "lynch": Peter Lynch (“One Up on Wall Street” and “Beating the Street”)
   "fisher": Philip Fisher (“Common Stocks and Uncommon Profits” (the 15 points, condensed))
   "graham": Benjamin Graham (“The Intelligent Investor”, criteria for the defensive investor)
   "thiel": Peter Thiel (“Zero to One”: the seven questions every business must answer)
   "gerstner": Brad Gerstner (His public letters (e.g. “Time to Get Fit”, 2022) and interviews (BG2 podcast); a summary, not an official checklist)
   "druckenmiller": Stanley Druckenmiller (His public interviews and speeches; a summary, not an official checklist)
   "smith": Terry Smith (Fundsmith owner's manual and annual letters (“buy good companies, don't overpay, do nothing”))
   "greenblatt": Joel Greenblatt (“The Little Book That Beats the Market” (the Magic Formula))
   "akre": Chuck Akre (Akre's “three-legged stool”)
   "pabrai": Mohnish Pabrai (“The Dhandho Investor”)

   "ackman": Bill Ackman (Pershing Square's stated investment criteria (annual letters and presentations))
   "sleep": Nick Sleep (Nomad Investment Partnership letters (2001–2014))
   "valentine": Don Valentine (His talks (e.g. Stanford GSB, 2010) on what Sequoia looks for)
   "nash": Tom Nash: the 12-step research process (“How to Find the Best Stocks in the Market” (Tom Nash, 2026))
 "checklist": { "<id>": {"verdict": "yes|partly|no|unknown", "evidence": "one specific sentence"} } for EVERY id below (each question is shared by the frameworks that ask it):
   "momentum": Has the share price risen strongly over roughly the last six to twelve months, beating the market?
   "g4": Is it run by great leaders and backed by smart, well-known investors or partners?
   "g6": Do commentators and analysts commonly call the stock overvalued (a trait Gardner sees as a good sign)?
   "simple": Is it an established business simple enough for a careful generalist to understand well?
   "b2": Has it shown consistent results over many years?
   "integrity": Is management honest and candid with shareholders, rational with capital, paid in a way that lines up with owners, and well governed?
   "b6": Does management avoid copying peers or empire-building for its own sake?
   "roic": Does it earn a high, consistent return on the capital it uses, without relying on debt?
   "fcf": Does it turn most of its profit into plenty of free cash flow?
   "b10": Has the money it kept (instead of paying out) grown the company's value by at least as much?
   "safety": Is the share price well below a conservative estimate of the business's value (a margin of safety)?
   "fairprice": Is the price reasonable for the quality and growth on offer?
   "mu5": Thinking backwards, are there few ways this business could fail?
   "reinvest": Can it reinvest its profits at high returns for many years?
   "ly2": Does it fit a clear category (fast grower, stalwart, turnaround…) with a simple story for its future?
   "ly3": Is the price/earnings ratio at or below the earnings growth rate?
   "runway": Can its sales keep growing substantially for many years, into new places or products?
   "ly7": Are insiders buying and is the company reducing its share count?
   "ly8": Is it overlooked by Wall Street or in a 'boring' niche?
   "fi2": Is management committed to developing new products as current ones mature?
   "fi3": Does its R&D spending produce results?
   "fi4": Is it unusually good at selling?
   "longterm": Does management put long-term value and innovation ahead of short-term profit?
   "gr1": Is it a large, established company?
   "ni10": Has it been profitable in each of the last ten years?
   "gr4": Has it paid a dividend every year for at least 20 years?
   "eps10": Has earnings per share grown by at least one third over ten years?
   "gr6": Is the share price no more than about 15 times average earnings?
   "gr7": Is price/earnings × price/book no more than about 22.5?
   "th1": Does it have proprietary technology about ten times better than the next best?
   "timing": Is the technology and market timing right for this business now?
   "th3": Did it start with a big share of a small market, and can it expand from there?
   "team": Is it led by an exceptional founder or world-class management team?
   "th5": Does it have a way to reach and sell to customers, not just a product?
   "durable": Will its market position still hold in 10 to 20 years, resisting disruption and obsolescence?
   "th7": Has it found a unique opportunity that others don't see?
   "trend": Is it a leading beneficiary of a major platform shift or secular trend (such as AI or cloud computing)?
   "dr1": Are earnings accelerating and analysts' estimates moving up?
   "dr2": Will the business look better in 18–24 months than today, beyond what is already obvious?
   "dr4": Do interest rates, central-bank liquidity and the economy work in its favour?
   "dr6": Are there identifiable events that could drive results higher?
   "dr7": Is conviction high enough that it could be a large, concentrated position?
   "gm": Is the gross margin high, a sign of pricing power?
   "fcfyield": Is the free-cash-flow yield reasonable or attractive for its quality and growth?
   "gb2": Is operating profit high compared with the whole company's value (enterprise value)?
   "pa2": Is the business or industry going through a temporary, fixable setback?
   "pa4": Is the chance of permanent loss small even if the outcome is uncertain?
   "wo1": Is it a leader in AI, robotics, energy storage, blockchain or multiomic sequencing?
   "wo2": Are its product costs falling quickly as volumes grow, opening up big new demand?
   "wo3": Does it combine several innovation platforms?
   "wo4": Could its addressable market be many times larger in five years?
   "ac3": Is it largely insulated from commodity prices, interest rates and similar outside forces?
   "ns1": Does it pass the savings from its growing size back to customers, making it ever harder to compete with?
   "ns4": Is its likely position in 10–20 years clearly stronger than today?
   "va2": Does the product solve a large, painful problem?
   "tn1": Does it sell into a real secular trend (like AI, energy or robotics; ideally the infrastructure layer), as a company built for that trend rather than an old business retrofitting?
   "tn2": Is there a gap between the story the market tells about the company and what it is actually becoming (like Palantir seen as a consultancy, Tesla as a car company)?
   "tn3": Is it outside the zones to avoid: small caps, Chinese companies, commodity producers, airlines, seasonal businesses and startups?
   "tn4": Of these three, does it pass at least two (and have a valid reason for any miss, such as infrastructure needing leverage or a clear path to profit): revenue grown for the past few years, profitable, more cash than debt?
   "tn5": Has free cash flow been positive, and cash exceeded debt, in each of the last 4 to 6 quarters?
   "tn6": Is revenue growing at 10% a year or more?
   "tn7": Is revenue growth % plus free-cash-flow margin % at least 40?
   "tn8": Over the last year, did revenue grow faster than total operating expenses?
   "tn9": Does it avoid every instant kill: market cap under $1B, more debt than cash, short interest above 10%, operating margin below 20%, revenue growth below 10% and falling, two or more earnings misses in the last 4 quarters, or less than 10 years since founding?
   "tn10": Is it free of any major regulatory or legal threat?
   "tn11": Can it be stated plainly as “provides X that helps Y achieve Z, and charges [revenue model]”, with a clear answer to what pain it cures, who is in pain, and why customers choose it over competitors?
   "tn13": Score it on Nash's 13 categories, 0, 5 or 10 each, using the last twelve months: cash vs debt (more debt / more cash / 2x+ cash), revenue growth (<10% / 10-20% / >20%), operating margin (<10% / 10-25% / >25%), short interest (>10% / 5-10% / <5%), institutional ownership (<30% / 30-60% / >60%), revenue growing faster than expenses (no 0 / yes 10), 5-year return vs the S&P 500 (behind / ahead by 10-20% / ahead by 20%+), and, judged harshly, moat, CEO, recession-proof pricing power, secular trend, culture and mission, talent (none / some / strong). Is the total 75 or more? Give the total in the evidence.
   "tn14": Over the last five years, has revenue grown every year, operating margin expanded, free cash flow been positive and rising, and cash exceeded debt every year?
   "tn15": Would a banker lend to it: interest coverage (operating income ÷ interest) of 4x or more, assets (excluding goodwill) at least 2× liabilities, current ratio of 1 or more, and total liabilities under 4× equity?
   "tn18": Does the CEO have a track record of execution (growth, margins, innovation), skin in the game through open-market share purchases, and 10+ years in the role, ideally as founder?
   "tn20": Has it consistently beaten earnings expectations?
   "tn21": Is it free of every red flag: a clown CEO, a co-CEO structure, an acquisition spree, any suspicion of fraud or accounting problems, an auditor change, declining margins, revenue spiking while inventory piles up, or insiders selling hard while the stock runs?
   "tn22": Does it avoid the hype trap of no revenue, weak fundamentals, constant share sales to raise cash and nonstop media hype?
   "tn24": Working back from today's price, is the growth the price implies below what the company is already delivering?
   "tn25": With Nash's DCF (3-year averages of revenue growth and FCF margin, trimmed growth, 5 years of free cash flow, 4% terminal growth, plus cash minus debt), is the value per share above today's price even at a 12% discount rate?
   "tn26": Using the multiple that fits (forward P/E vs peers for mature companies, hardware and banks; Rule of 40 for software; price to sales vs the industry for unprofitable growth), is it attractive, with a PEG (forward P/E ÷ EPS growth) of 1 or less?
 "asOf": "YYYY-MM"}

summaries.gardner: GE Aerospace is the top dog in commercial jet engines with a strong CEO and a stock up roughly fivefold over five years, but it is a century-old company in a mature industry rather than an emerging one. It fits Gardner's quality and leadership traits better than his 'important emerging industry' trait, and the stock has stalled over the past year.
summaries.buffett: It has a durable moat (a $190.6B backlog, mostly long-term services on about 50,000 installed commercial engines) and rational, candid management under Larry Culp. The weak points for a Buffett lens are the conglomerate's erratic ten-year record, leverage against a $17.6B equity base and a price near 40 times forward earnings, which leaves no margin of safety.
summaries.munger: The razor-and-blades engine model, high switching costs and a three-player industry are the kind of simple, durable economics Munger liked. Inverting, the failure modes are a major engine safety problem, LEAP durability costs and a slower aftermarket cycle, but the main objection is paying a full price for a great business.
summaries.lynch: Lynch would classify GE Aerospace as a successful turnaround that has become a stalwart-to-fast-grower, with adjusted EPS guided up about 20%+ in 2026. The story is easy to tell, but with a P/E near 40 versus EPS growth of roughly 20%, the PEG is about 2, above his preferred level, and the stock is anything but overlooked.
summaries.fisher: GE fits Fisher's growth criteria well: long product runways (LEAP ramp, GE9X, RISE open fan), about $3.0B a year of R&D, an unmatched installed-base sales position and a lean-management culture. Lower marks come from cyclical exposure to airlines and Boeing's production problems.
summaries.graham: GE fails most of Graham's defensive-investor tests: it had losses in 2017, 2018 and 2021, its dividend was cut to a penny in 2018, and the shares trade at about 40 times earnings and about 18 times book value. It is a large company, but nothing about the price meets Graham's standards.
summaries.thiel: GE/CFM enjoys a near-monopoly position on key platforms (sole engine on the 737 MAX and 777X) and decades of proprietary materials know-how, with distribution through its installed base. It is not a zero-to-one startup story, and its technology lead over Pratt & Whitney and Rolls-Royce is meaningful but not tenfold.
summaries.gerstner: Gerstner-style focus on durable growth, operating discipline and capital returns is matched by GE's 18% revenue growth in 2025, margin expansion and heavy buybacks. The concern would be valuation: a forward P/E near 40 and a free-cash-flow yield under 3% leave little room for error.
summaries.druckenmiller: Earnings are accelerating (2026 adjusted EPS guidance raised to $7.65-$7.85) and the commercial aerospace cycle remains strong, but the stock has lagged since its August 2026 high as analysts like Melius warned of slower aftermarket growth in 2027. The liquidity-driven, momentum-based setup Druckenmiller looks for is weaker now than in 2024-2025.
summaries.smith: GE Aerospace now looks like a 'good company' in Terry Smith's sense: high returns on its operating assets, strong cash conversion (free cash flow of $7.7B in 2025, 113% conversion) and a long runway. It fails 'don't overpay' at about 40 times forward earnings and a sub-3% free-cash-flow yield.
summaries.greenblatt: On the Magic Formula, operating profit is only about 3% of an enterprise value of roughly $330B, so the earnings yield is low. Return on tangible capital is high, but the combined rank would be poor at today's price.
summaries.akre: GE scores well on Akre's first two legs: an extraordinary business with a services annuity and a capable, owner-minded manager in Culp. The third leg, reinvestment, is mixed because much of the cash goes to buybacks and dividends rather than high-return internal reinvestment, and the price is full.
summaries.pabrai: Pabrai's Dhandho approach wants a durable moat bought at a deep discount with low downside; GE has the moat but not the discount. There is no temporary setback depressing the price, so the 'heads I win, tails I don't lose much' setup is missing.
summaries.wood: GE is not a disruptive-innovation platform in ARK's sense; jet engines are a mature technology with incremental efficiency gains. Open-fan and hybrid-electric propulsion and additive manufacturing are innovative, but they are not the exponential cost-decline platforms ARK targets.
summaries.ackman: GE fits much of Pershing Square's checklist: a simple, predictable, free-cash-flow-generating business with high barriers to entry and strong management, and Ackman has praised GE's transformation publicly. Leverage relative to book equity and the high valuation would temper the case today.
summaries.sleep: Nick Sleep looked for scale economics shared with customers; GE's scale advantage is real but it keeps much of the benefit through rising spare-part prices rather than passing it on. Its position is durable, but it is not the 'scale economics shared' model of Costco or Amazon.
summaries.valentine: Valentine sought huge markets and technology-driven startups; GE Aerospace operates in a large, growing market but is a mature incumbent, not a venture opportunity. Its painful-problem solution (reliable, efficient propulsion) is clear, but the framework fits poorly.
summaries.nash: GE sells into the secular growth of air travel and defense, beats earnings consistently and has strong margins, scoring about 100 of 130 on Nash's categories. But it fails his instant-kill and banker tests because borrowings of $19.2B exceed cash of $9.3B, and his DCF values it well below the current price.

momentum.evidence: The share price was about $307.63 in October 2026, roughly flat versus about $309 in October 2025 and about 21% below its August 6, 2026 intraday record of $388.84.

g4.evidence: CEO Larry Culp, former Danaher CEO, led GE's breakup into three companies, and GE is widely held by large institutions.

g6.evidence: Commentators frequently debate GE's valuation at about 38-40 times forward earnings, above peers like TransDigm (about 24x), and Melius downgraded it to Hold in September 2026.

simple.evidence: It sells jet engines and then earns decades of service and spare-part revenue; CES was about 73% of 2025 revenue with services 75% of CES.

b2.evidence: GE Aerospace has grown steadily since 2022, but the old GE had large losses in 2017, 2018 and 2021 and a 2018 dividend cut.

integrity.evidence: Culp's guidance has been conservative and repeatedly raised, he bought GE shares in May 2022, and capital allocation (debt reduction, spin-offs, buybacks) has been disciplined.

b6.evidence: Management shrank the empire by spinning off GE HealthCare (2023) and GE Vernova (2024) to focus on aerospace.

roic.evidence: Returns on operating capital are high (2025 operating profit $9.1B on modest tangible capital), but book equity of $17.6B is small relative to $109.8B of liabilities, which includes run-off insurance reserves and borrowings.

fcf.evidence: 2025 free cash flow was $7.7B, 113% of adjusted net income.

b10.evidence: Since 2022, retained capital plus buybacks have coincided with a large rise in market value, but over the past decade the old GE destroyed large amounts of value.

safety.evidence: At about $307.63 the stock trades near 40 times 2026 adjusted EPS guidance of $7.65-$7.85 and above a conservative DCF value.

fairprice.evidence: The forward P/E near 38-40 is high for an industrial, though earnings are growing about 20% a year and the business quality is exceptional.

mu5.evidence: The services annuity makes outright failure unlikely, but an engine safety crisis, a grounding or a sharp aerospace downturn (as in 2020) could badly hurt results.

reinvest.evidence: It reinvests in R&D ($1.58B self-funded in 2025) and capacity, but most cash goes to buybacks ($7.55B in 2025) and dividends ($1.45B).

ly2.evidence: It is a completed turnaround becoming a stalwart/fast grower, powered by the LEAP fleet entering high-margin shop visits.

ly3.evidence: Forward P/E of about 39-40 is roughly double the expected adjusted EPS growth of about 20%.

runway.evidence: Total remaining performance obligation was $190.6B at end-2025, and LEAP shop visits will grow for years as the fleet ages.

ly7.evidence: Diluted shares fell from 1,099m (2023) to 1,047m (Q2 2026) through buybacks, but insiders have not made notable open-market purchases since Culp's May 2022 buys.

ly8.evidence: GE is a roughly $320B mega-cap followed by about 20 analysts.

fi2.evidence: It is developing the CFM RISE open-fan engine, GE9X for the 777X, adaptive-cycle military engines and hybrid-electric demonstrators.

fi3.evidence: Past R&D produced the LEAP, now sole engine on the 737 MAX, and the GE9X, the world's most powerful certified commercial jet engine.

fi4.evidence: 2025 orders rose 32% to $66.2B and services make up $163.0B of the $190.6B backlog.

longterm.evidence: GE keeps funding decade-long programs like RISE and accepts losses on new LEAP engines to build an installed base that pays back over 25-30 years.

gr1.evidence: 2025 revenue was $45,855m and market value is about $320B.

ni10.evidence: GE reported net losses in 2017, 2018 and 2021.

gr4.evidence: GE has paid a dividend every year for well over 20 years, though it cut the quarterly payout to $0.01 in 2018.

eps10.evidence: The breakups, the 2021 1-for-8 reverse split and losses in several years make a like-for-like ten-year EPS comparison unreliable.

gr6.evidence: The price is about 38 times 2025 diluted EPS of $8.14, far above 15 times average earnings.

gr7.evidence: With P/E near 38 and price-to-book near 18 (market value about $319B vs equity of $17.6B), the product is far above 22.5.

th1.evidence: LEAP and GE9X lead on efficiency and durability, but they are not ten times better than Pratt & Whitney or Rolls-Royce engines.

timing.evidence: Record air traffic, aircraft backlogs of over 15,000 jets and the LEAP fleet's first major shop visits make the timing favourable.

th3.evidence: It long ago grew into a dominant share of a large market rather than starting from a small niche.

team.evidence: Culp is widely regarded as one of the best industrial CEOs for turning around and breaking up GE since 2018.

th5.evidence: Its installed base of about 50,000 commercial engines and long-term service agreements give it direct, recurring access to every major airline.

durable.evidence: Engines sold today will fly into the 2050s, and only three Western companies can make large jet engines.

th7.evidence: Its opportunity (engine aftermarket) is well understood by investors and rivals.

trend.evidence: It benefits from the secular growth of air travel and higher defense spending, not from AI or cloud computing.

dr1.evidence: In July 2026 GE raised 2026 adjusted EPS guidance to $7.65-$7.85 from $7.10-$7.40 after 23% first-half revenue growth, though some analysts have since trimmed 2027 views.

dr2.evidence: Rising LEAP shop visits and deliveries should lift results, but slower CFM56 retirements and Melius's warning of high-single-digit aftermarket growth in 2027 are already debated.

dr4.evidence: Strong airline traffic and defense budgets help, but high rates and tariffs weigh on airline economics and supply chains.

dr6.evidence: Upcoming catalysts include Q3 2026 results, Boeing and Airbus production rate increases, and 777X/GE9X entry into service.

dr7.evidence: Business quality supports high conviction, but the valuation and Boeing-related risks argue against an outsized position.

gm.evidence: Gross margin on equipment and services was about 31.6% in 2025, solid for an industrial but not software-like.

fcfyield.evidence: Trailing free cash flow of about $8.8B against a market value of about $319B is a yield under 3%.

gb2.evidence: Operating profit of about $10B is only about 3% of an enterprise value near $330B.

pa2.evidence: There is no fixable setback depressing the business; results are at record levels.

pa4.evidence: The business is very unlikely to fail, but at about 40 times earnings a permanent loss from multiple compression is possible.

wo1.evidence: It is not a leader in AI, robotics, energy storage, blockchain or multiomics.

wo2.evidence: LEAP unit costs fall as production rises, but this lowers GE's losses on new engines rather than opening big new demand.

wo3.evidence: Additive manufacturing is its only ARK-style innovation platform.

wo4.evidence: Its addressable market grows at mid-to-high single digits, not many-fold in five years.

ac3.evidence: Services revenue is resilient, but air traffic, oil prices and material costs (nickel, titanium) affect demand and costs, as 2020 showed.

ns1.evidence: GE raises spare-part prices annually rather than passing scale savings to customers.

ns4.evidence: As the LEAP fleet ages, the service annuity should be larger in 10-20 years than today.

va2.evidence: Reliable, fuel-efficient propulsion for commercial and military aircraft is a large and critical problem.

tn1.evidence: It sells into the growth of air travel and defense as the infrastructure layer (engines), but it is an old business rather than one built for a new trend.

tn2.evidence: Some still see 'old GE', but the market has largely re-rated it as a pure-play aerospace services franchise.

tn3.evidence: It is a US mega-cap, not a small cap, Chinese company, commodity producer, airline, seasonal business or startup.

tn4.evidence: It passes two of three: revenue grew from $29,139m (2022) to $45,855m (2025) and it is profitable, but borrowings ($19.2B) exceed cash ($9.3B).

tn5.evidence: Free cash flow has been positive each quarter, but borrowings ($19.2B at June 30, 2026; $20.5B at end-2025) exceeded cash in each period.

tn6.evidence: GAAP revenue grew 18.5% in 2025 and 23% in the first half of 2026.

tn7.evidence: 2025 revenue growth of 18.5% plus a free-cash-flow margin of about 16.8% ($7.7B / $45.9B) is about 35, below 40; first-half 2026 growth of 23% plus about 18% FCF margin is about 41.

tn8.evidence: In 2025 total revenue rose 18.5% while total costs and expenses rose 12.0% ($33,346m to $37,342m).

tn9.evidence: It trips the 'more debt than cash' kill: borrowings of $19.2B vs cash of $9.3B at June 30, 2026.

tn10.evidence: There is no existential legal threat, but FAA scrutiny (e.g. the September 2026 737 MAX 10 delay tied to a GE-supplied software fault), tariffs and export controls are real risks.

tn11.evidence: GE provides jet engines and services that help airlines and militaries fly safely and efficiently, charging for engines and then decades of parts and service contracts; customers choose it for fuel efficiency, reliability and the global service network.

tn13.evidence: Total about 100/130: cash vs debt 0, revenue growth 10, operating margin 5 (21.4%), short interest 10, institutional ownership 10, revenue faster than expenses 10, 5-year return vs S&P 10, moat 10, CEO 10, pricing power 10, secular trend 5, culture/mission 5, talent 5.

tn14.evidence: Revenue and margins have risen since 2022, but borrowings exceeded cash in recent years and the pre-2022 record belongs to the old conglomerate.

tn15.evidence: Interest coverage is strong (about 11x: $9.1B operating profit vs $843m interest), but liabilities are 6.2x equity ($109.8B vs $17.6B), the current ratio is 0.98 and assets excluding goodwill are only 1.08x liabilities.

tn18.evidence: Culp has a strong execution record since 2018 and bought shares in May 2022, but he is not a founder and has led GE for about 8 years.

tn20.evidence: GE beat EPS expectations in each quarter of 2025 and in Q1 and Q2 2026, raising guidance each time.

tn21.evidence: No accounting or auditor red flags and margins are rising, but GE has a long history of accounting issues (2020 SEC settlement of $200m) under prior management.

tn22.evidence: It has $45.9B of revenue, strong profits and is buying back stock rather than selling it.

tn24.evidence: At about 40 times forward earnings and a sub-3% free-cash-flow yield, the price implies sustained high growth above what a conservative DCF supports.

tn25.evidence: Using about 15% growth and a 13% FCF margin (3-year averages), 4% terminal growth and a 12% discount rate gives roughly $111B, about $106 per share, far below the $307.63 price.

tn26.evidence: Forward P/E of about 38-40 is in line with Howmet (~40x) but well above TransDigm (~24x), and with EPS growth near 20% the PEG is about 2.
